I am trying to build a sorting algorithm in Python that sorts a list of integers in O(n log n) time. Can you help me implement merge sort?

Claude responded: Sure! Merge sort is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm that runs in O(n log n) time.

Sure! Merge sort is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm that runs in O(n log n) time. Here is a clean Python implementation:

def merge_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
    return merge(left, right)

def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

The time complexity is O(n log n) in all cases, and the space complexity is O(n) because we create new arrays during merging.

Claude responded: Of course! Here are some tests using Python's unittest module:

Of course! Here are some tests using Python's unittest module:

import unittest

class TestMergeSort(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_empty(self):
        self.assertEqual(merge_sort([]), [])
    def test_single(self):
        self.assertEqual(merge_sort([1]), [1])
    def test_sorted(self):
        self.assertEqual(merge_sort([1, 2, 3]), [1, 2, 3])
    def test_reverse(self):
        self.assertEqual(merge_sort([3, 2, 1]), [1, 2, 3])
